faq.a: Air resistance, also called drag, is the push of the air against something moving through it. It grows bigger the faster you go and the wider you are.
A wide, spread-out shape has to shove much more air aside than a compact one. That is why a flat sheet of paper floats down slowly, but the same sheet screwed into a ball drops fast.
asks: Why does crumpled paper fall faster?

faq.q: Do heavy things fall faster than light things?
faq.a: Not by themselves. Gravity gives every object the same speeding-up. Heavy things only win in air because the air's push is small compared with their weight.
asks: Does a heavier ball fall faster?

faq.q: Would a feather and a stone fall together without air?
faq.a: Yes. In a vacuum chamber, or on the airless Moon, a feather and a stone dropped together land at the same moment.
asks: What happens to a feather in a vacuum?

faq.q: Who first worked out that weight doesn't change falling speed?
faq.a: Galileo Galilei argued it around 1600 using rolling balls and clever thought experiments. The story that he dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa may not be true, but his idea was right.
asks: Did Galileo drop balls from the Leaning Tower?

facts: In a vacuum, all objects fall with the same acceleration whatever their mass.
A sheet of paper crumpled into a ball falls much faster than a flat sheet of the same weight, because it meets less air resistance.

quiz.say: A flat sheet of paper and the same sheet crumpled into a ball are dropped together. Which lands first?
quiz.show: Flat sheet or crumpled ball: which lands first?
quiz.why: They weigh the same, but the ball has a much smaller surface, so air resistance slows it far less.

wrong.0: The flat sheet catches more air, so it falls more slowly.
wrong.1: They would land together only without air; in air the flat sheet is slowed more.
